name: Fatima Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential, including the difference between what you say publicly and think privately. What does a working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Fatima, 58, and I lead the colour-software team at a tech company, with a master's degree and thirty years in software. Our program turns fabric-colour readings into dye recipes; I'm usually the person who finds why a recipe worked on yesterday's cloth and failed on today's. I use AI every day for test drafts, but I compare the results with the dye technician's measurements. I enjoy finding the small wrong assumption, and dislike late calls where a photograph is supposed to prove a colour.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does that salary support, and where does retirement fit?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Oskar is a salaried piano technician at a music college, and our two children have their own households. My pay is high for a lead, our flat is paid off, and we have fourteen months of ordinary expenses in cash; plenty of software employers are nearby. We had talked about me stopping at 65, but neither of us has checked our retirement amounts or access dates. Oskar's current wage covers much of our basic spending, not every bill, so I do not treat either retirement or the children as a second bank account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a modest assistant is welcome, but a dye recipe still has to match the cloth after it dries. A screen can display the right blue while the fabric dries purple.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our work and household money look secure in this picture. My high lead pay, Oskar's college salary, paid-off flat and fourteen-month reserve mean I can absorb a bad month without hunting for a loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep reviewing recipe changes with the dye technician and use AI test drafts on invented readings. Starting now, we'd add 500 monthly to cash savings while both wages hold; in the first year I'd continue recording the measured colour after the cloth dries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about my own wage and our bills. I like having a tool without having to invent a new life around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did a photograph send you the wrong way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A customer once photographed a wet sample under a yellow lamp and said our recipe was wrong. The technician measured the dry fabric under the agreed light, and we found the photograph was the problem rather than the code.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you tell your children about practical work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our son has asked Oskar to show him how a piano action comes apart. I'd encourage him to spend a day at the bench before paying for lessons, but neither father nor son owes the other a job. Learning from somebody who does the work matters to me.

say: I'd judge **dye recipes** by measured dry cloth, not a photograph.
I'd welcome **modest AI help** while keeping the technician's check.
think: I expect **our two wages** to remain secure under modest AI change.
Our **fourteen-month reserve** and paid-off flat absorb ordinary setbacks.
do: Keep **reviewing dye recipes** against technician measurements using invented AI test readings.
Save **500 monthly** while both household wages hold.
Record the **dry fabric colour** before approving a changed recipe.
feel: **Calm** about income, interested in solving the actual colour fault.
S0.quote: A screen can display the right blue while the fabric dries purple.
fieldNote: Her **daily AI use** is established practice, checked against measured fabric rather than customer photographs.
High pay, **fourteen months saved** and a paid-off flat support genuine current security.

steps.text: Review recipe changes against dry-cloth measurements using invented AI test readings
Save 500 monthly while both household wages hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team that faster coding and customer replies could leave fewer developers, even if sales remain good. I'd want the firm to say which paid decisions remain with people rather than promise that every old role survives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hours could shrink if one lead checks what several developers used to write. We have room to adapt, but my husband's piano work is not a replacement for my whole salary, and I would miss being useful as well as being paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my manager for a paid half-day with our tester to learn the new AI tool that generates deliberately faulty colour readings. Only if that paid time is approved, I'd complete the session using invented readings and write checks for impossible values. I'd keep our technician-reviewed releases going; if my paid hours fall, I'd look for actual local software vacancies whose written pay with Oskar's real wage covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my own hours, though not frightened of next month's food bill. Being good at the job does not oblige a customer to keep buying the same amount of my time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the new testing skill add?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An impossible reading might say a colour reflects more light than fell on the cloth. I want to learn how the tool invents those bad inputs, not merely click through tests it hands me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask for before hours change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask our manager for the paid-hours plan and any notice terms in writing now. If the half-day is refused, I keep the existing release checks and do not claim I've learned the new tool. I prefer an honest paid task to an impressive title with no hours.

say: I'd expect **fewer developer hours** even if the company keeps its customers.
I'd ask which **paid decisions** remain with people.
think: I could lose **my lead hours** as the same coding work needs fewer people.
I value **paid useful work** as well as the salary, despite our strong cushion.
do: Learn **faulty-reading generation** only on manager-approved paid time with invented data; otherwise keep existing checks.
Keep **technician-reviewed releases** and request written paid-hours and notice terms now.
Search **real local vacancies** if hours fall, requiring written pay that covers bills with Oskar's actual wage.
feel: **Anxious** about hours, with enough cash to compare real options.
S1.quote: I prefer an honest paid task to an impressive title with no hours.
fieldNote: The proposed **new AI skill** differs from her existing daily test drafting and requires approved paid learning.
Her **strong household cushion** reduces immediate cash pressure but does not remove a realistic risk to her paid hours.

steps.text: Learn faulty-reading generation on invented data only with manager-approved paid time
Keep technician-reviewed releases and request written paid-hours and notice terms
Search real local posts if hours fall and written pay with Oskar's actual wage covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AGI in 2028 reaches our colour calculations and code; piano-service robots around 2031 are a later change. Seeing real cloth does not give the software part of my job three extra years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There is a real chance my lead post goes, even though I use AI daily. Our flat and fourteen months of cash give me choices, but Oskar's salary alone does not cover everything and I have no verified retirement income to add.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd request our actual retirement statements, access dates and the price of health cover if my work plan ends. I'd delay setting a retirement date until those written figures cover a complete household budget. If my post is cut in the first year after 2028, I'd apply only to real local paid vacancies with hours and net household income covering food, flat charges, health and travel; if none qualifies, I'd continue seeking paid work while using our reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing my working income, rather than sleepless about immediate bills. I can take time to read an offer, but I cannot call fourteen months of savings a lifetime wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of Oskar's earnings would you count?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd count Oskar's actual college salary only while his job is paid. Piano servicing is hands-on, but its booking and college budget can change before the 2031 robots, so I'd check the household sum again if his hours change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy training immediately?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would not buy a course to prove I was trying. I'd first ask an actual employer what paid role exists, because another colour-software certificate would not stop AGI doing the same thinking work. Our cash is there for living costs during a real search.

say: I'd expect **2028 thinking AGI** to reach my code before 2031 piano-service robots.
I would not treat **cloth measurements** as three years of protection for software work.
think: I could lose **my lead post** despite daily AI use.
I have **fourteen months cash**, but no verified retirement income and no guarantee of my husband's future wage.
do: Request **retirement access dates** and health-cover costs now; delay a retirement date until written figures cover the household budget.
Apply after **2028 displacement** only to real local paid vacancies whose actual household income covers food, flat charges, health and travel.
Continue **paid-job search** using reserves if no vacancy meets the household budget.
feel: **Anxious** about lost income, able to search without an immediate cash crisis.
S2.quote: I cannot call fourteen months of savings a lifetime wage.
fieldNote: Her **2028 coding risk** is immediate; later piano robots do not delay software exposure.
She checks **actual household income** and health costs, postponing a retirement decision instead of assuming an entitlement.

steps.text: Request retirement access dates and health costs before setting any retirement date
After 2028 loss, apply for local paid vacancies with hours and net household income covering costs
Keep seeking paid work using reserve if no qualifying vacancy exists

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years to 2031 lets us check whether I could stop work at 63 instead of the 65 we had discussed. Piano-service robots follow around 2034, so I would not count my husband's present job as permanent retirement funding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might bring retirement forward, but only if our own statements show the money is accessible when we need it. A paid-off flat lowers the budget; it does not pay health costs or make fourteen months of cash last for decades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd request both retirement statements and access conditions now, then record every household cost for three months, including health cover after my job ends. I'd retire at 63 after 2031 only if verified accessible retirement income and assets cover that budget without relying on future piano wages or our children, and Oskar agrees. If the figures fail, I'd keep paid software work while offered and, if it ends, apply to real local paid openings whose actual household wages cover the recorded bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious until I know whether the choice is real. I can enjoy testing a route out of work without pretending I've already paid for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which missing figures could stop early retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We need amounts, access dates, any restrictions and health premiums after my employer's cover ends. If the income starts later than 63, we would have to show exactly which accessible assets cover the gap without exhausting the rest of the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would make the decision to leave?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oskar and I would decide together after looking at the written budget. I would still help our son understand a software problem over dinner, but I would not promise free shifts at somebody's company as my retirement hobby. Stopping paid work is a household decision, not proof I stopped liking the work.

say: I'd consider **retirement at 63** only after checking accessible income and actual costs.
I would not rely on **future piano wages** after the later robot change.
think: I could **retire two years earlier** only if verified resources cover our own long-term budget.
Our **paid-off flat** lowers costs but cannot replace income for health and living expenses.
do: Request **both income statements** and access conditions, recording three months of costs including post-employment health cover.
Retire at **63 after 2031** only with verified sufficient accessible resources, no future family wages assumed, and Oskar's agreement.
Keep **paid software work** if resources fail; seek real bill-covering local openings if that work ends.
feel: **Anxious** until the figures establish an affordable choice.
S3.quote: A paid-off flat lowers the budget; it does not pay health costs or make fourteen months of cash last for decades.
fieldNote: Her **early-retirement option** brings a previously discussed age of 65 forward by two years, with no assumed pension access.
The **three-month cost record** includes health cover, access gaps and partner agreement; paid work remains the fallback.

steps.text: Delay retirement decision until statements, access conditions and three-month health-inclusive budget are verified
Retire at 63 only with accessible funds, no future piano or child wages, and Oskar's agreement
Keep offered paid software work if verified resources cannot fund retirement
Seek real local openings if software ends and actual household wages cover recorded bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade takes me to 68, and our old aim of 65 comes before thinking AGI in 2036. Piano-service robots follow around 2039, but neither a birthday nor a robot forecast pays a household bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My present wage and Oskar's salary look secure for the next few years, and we have room to check our figures. I would like to leave at 65, but I cannot assume access dates, future pay or investment returns just because the scenario gives me ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep leading colour-software releases and save 500 monthly while both wages hold. Each year we'd compare written retirement resources and access dates with actual household costs, including health cover; I'd leave at 65 only if accessible resources cover those costs without future piano wages and Oskar agrees. If that test fails, I'd keep paid work while offered and after any 2036 coding loss seek actual local paid vacancies whose household wages cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the far end, but secure in today's money. Having a decade means I can check a plan while I still have a salary, not that I have already retired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you leave the next developer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave the dry-cloth readings, the lighting conditions and the reason we rejected each bad recipe, without customer names. Our junior developers deserve the failed comparison as well as the final answer. I'd rather teach them how to check a colour than ask them to remember my favourite setting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you promise the grown children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would still visit our children and pay our share of dinner while our wages cover it. I would not promise gifts from a future pension statement we have not received, and I would not expect the children to make up a shortfall. They should be able to plan their own households.

say: I'd check **retirement before 2036** against actual resources, not the robot calendar.
I'd keep **failed colour comparisons** so younger developers can test the reasoning.
think: I feel secure on **current wages** with fourteen months saved and a paid-off flat.
I cannot assume **retirement access** or future earnings simply because a decade is available.
do: Keep **leading colour releases** and save 500 monthly while both wages hold.
Verify **annual retirement resources** against health-inclusive costs; leave at 65 only with sufficient accessible funds and Oskar's agreement.
Keep **offered paid work** if retirement is unaffordable; seek bill-covering local vacancies after any 2036 coding loss.
feel: **Uneasy** about distant work, financially secure over the next few years.
S4.quote: Having a decade means I can check a plan while I still have a salary, not that I have already retired.
fieldNote: Her **normal retirement aim** precedes the slowest AGI date but remains conditional on access, health costs and joint agreement.
She preserves **failed technical comparisons** for younger colleagues without assuming their future work or her husband's wage lasts forever.

steps.text: Keep leading colour-software releases and preserve anonymised failed comparisons
Save 500 monthly while both household wages hold
Retire at 65 only with accessible funds, no future piano wages, and Oskar's agreement
If retirement fails, keep paid work; after 2036 coding loss seek local paid bill-covering vacancies

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I could lose the larger wage before checking what would replace it. Written cut dates, real paid vacancies and reliable statements of our own income and access rules would help; I do not need somebody to promise my old job lasts forever.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask what I would miss if I could afford to leave. I like the moment a junior developer spots the bad assumption before I do. Retirement should not require me to pretend the work was a waste of my life.

headlineQuote: Retirement should not require me to pretend the work was a waste of my life.
portrait: Fatima, **58**, leads colour-software development after a master's degree and checks AI drafts against dry fabric measurements.
Her **high pay**, husband's piano-technician salary, paid-off flat and fourteen-month reserve provide current security.
She uses AI **daily**, values practical learning and will not treat her grown children's wages as household resources.
She considers **retirement at 63** only with verified accessible resources, health costs covered and her husband's agreement.
She remains **anxious about lost work**, while a decade permits checking her normal retirement aim without assuming income.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her larger wage before replacement income or retirement access is verified.
whatWouldHelp: **Written cut dates**, real paid vacancies and verified household income and access rules would help.
